analysis.one_liner: Lets antitrust enforcers fine drug companies that file baseless FDA petitions to delay cheaper generic competitors.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 31-9 with bipartisan sponsorship, but it never received a vote by the full House and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes file petitions with the FDA claiming safety or manufacturing problems with a rival's application to sell a generic copy of their drug. Some of these petitions have no real basis and exist mainly to run out the clock, keeping a cheaper generic off the market. This bill declares such baseless petitions an unfair method of competition under antitrust law and lets the Federal Trade Commission sue the filer, with penalties of up to $50,000 per day of delay or the revenue the brand company earned while the generic was held up.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who would get access to cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars sooner, and generic drug makers whose applications would face fewer delay tactics. Faster generic competition is one of the main ways prescription drug prices come down.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair method of competition, enforceable by the FTC, to submit an objectively baseless FDA petition for the purpose of interfering with a competitor's application for a generic drug or biosimilar [S2, S3].

Sets a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for each day the FDA spent reviewing a sham petition, or alternatively the brand company's revenue from the drug during the delay — a penalty designed to make delay tactics unprofitable [S2, S3].

Creates a presumption that a petition is part of a sham series when the Secretary of Health and Human Services finds it was filed primarily to delay approval, shifting the burden to the drug company to prove otherwise [S3].

The bill's stated purpose includes facilitating efficient review of petitions filed in good faith to raise legitimate public health concerns, so it targets delay tactics rather than the petition process itself [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would face antitrust liability and large penalties for filing petitions that courts find baseless, and which would lose the months or years of extra brand-price sales they currently gain by delaying generic entry.

drawbacks.text: Legitimate safety petitions could be chilled: a company that raises a genuine quality or manufacturing concern about a generic now risks an FTC lawsuit, and defenders of the petition process argue some petitions that look like delay raise real issues the FDA needs to hear [S3].

The penalty structure is unusually harsh for an antitrust remedy — a per-day fine of $50,000 or the filer's full drug revenue during the delay period — and even supporters would acknowledge it will be tested in court and could produce years of litigation before it changes behavior [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to anyone who fills a prescription: earlier generic competition reliably lowers drug prices, and the bill keeps the petition process open for good-faith safety concerns. The main cost is the risk of over-deterring legitimate petitions, which the drafters tried to limit by requiring that a petition be 'objectively baseless' and by preserving all other antitrust remedies. On balance the design targets a documented delay tactic while leaving ordinary petitions alone.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it 31-9 in September 2021, but House leadership never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, joined by original cosponsors including Republicans Ken Buck and judiciary members Jerrold Nadler, David Cicilline, and Carolyn Maloney [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction [S5].
On September 29, 2021, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill to be reported in the nature of a substitute by a vote of 31-9 [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the bill was never scheduled for a vote by the full House and died at the end of the 117th Congress [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: they keep the ability to file petitions against generic competitors with no antitrust penalty risk, and patients keep paying brand-name prices for drugs whose cheaper copies are delayed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 8 cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 3 Republicans, and the committee approved it 31-9, but no floor vote ever occurred where party positions could be recorded [S4, S5].

industries.note: These companies use FDA citizen petitions to delay generic and biosimilar competitors, preserving months or years of brand-price sales; the bill would make baseless delay petitions an antitrust violation carrying penalties up to $50,000 per day or the revenue earned during the delay [S2, S3].
Their applications would face fewer sham petitions, letting cheaper copies reach patients sooner and expanding their market [S2, S3].
